acceptedAnswer.text: Java HashMap is a hash table-based implementation of the Map interface in the java.util package. It stores key-value pairs and uses a hash function to determine the storage bucket for each key. HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values, is not synchronized (not thread-safe), and does not guarantee any iteration order. It offers O(1) average-case performance for get() and put() operations. Introduced in Java 1.2 as part of the Collections Framework, it is the most widely used Map implementation in Java.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between HashMap and Hashtable in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Key differences: (1) Thread Safety — HashMap is not synchronized; Hashtable is synchronized (all methods). (2) Null Handling — HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values; Hashtable allows neither. (3) Performance — HashMap is faster in single-threaded code due to zero synchronization overhead. (4) Legacy — Hashtable is a legacy class from Java 1.0 extending Dictionary; HashMap was added in Java 1.2 extending AbstractMap. (5) Initial Capacity — HashMap defaults to 16 (power of two); Hashtable defaults to 11 (prime). (6) Iteration — HashMap uses fail-fast Iterator; Hashtable supports both Enumeration (legacy) and Iterator.

mainEntity.name: How does HashMap handle collisions in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: HashMap handles collisions using separate chaining — each bucket holds a linked list of entries that hash to the same bucket index. In Java 8+, when a single bucket's chain grows beyond 8 entries (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD) and the total table capacity is at least 64, the linked list is converted into a balanced Red-Black Tree, improving worst-case lookup from O(n) to O(log n). When entries are removed and the tree shrinks below 6 nodes (UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD), it converts back to a linked list.

mainEntity.name: Can HashMap have null keys or null values?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. HashMap allows exactly one null key and any number of null values. The null key is always stored in bucket 0 (index 0), bypassing the normal hash computation since null has no hashCode(). Null values are stored normally. This is in contrast to Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap, both of which throw NullPointerException for null keys or null values.

mainEntity.name: What is the default capacity and load factor of HashMap?

acceptedAnswer.text: HashMap's default initial capacity is 16 (a power of two) and the default load factor is 0.75. The initial threshold is 16 × 0.75 = 12, meaning rehashing is triggered when the 13th entry is inserted. During rehashing, the bucket array doubles in size (e.g., 16 → 32 → 64 → ...), always remaining a power of two. This power-of-two sizing enables fast bitwise AND bucket-index computation instead of the slower modulo operation used by Hashtable.

blocks.text: Java HashMap is the most widely used implementation of the Map<K, V> interface in the Java Collections Framework. Introduced in Java 1.2, it stores data as key-value pairs inside an internal array of buckets (nodes), using a hash function to compute where each entry belongs. It provides O(1) average-case time complexity for get() and put() operations — making it the default go-to Map for everyday Java development.

Unlike its ancestor Hashtable, HashMap is not synchronized and therefore not inherently thread-safe. It is designed for single-threaded use or scenarios where external synchronization is managed by the developer. This deliberate design choice eliminates lock overhead and makes it significantly faster than Hashtable in single-threaded workloads.

HashMap stands apart from other Map implementations with two key permissions: it allows exactly one null key (always stored at bucket index 0) and any number of null values. It does not maintain insertion order (use LinkedHashMap for that) and does not sort keys (use TreeMap for that). Iteration order is undefined and can change after a rehash.

A landmark improvement came in Java 8: when a single bucket's linked-list chain exceeds 8 nodes (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD) and the overall table capacity is at least 64, that chain is automatically converted into a Red-Black Tree. This brings worst-case lookup for hash-colliding keys from O(n) down to O(log n) — a critical fix for adversarial inputs designed to create hash collisions.

sections.title: Internal Structure — How HashMap Works Under the Hood

blocks.text: HashMap internally maintains an array of Node objects. Each Node is the head of a singly linked list — or, in Java 8+, a Red-Black Tree — of entries that map to the same bucket index. This collision-resolution strategy is called separate chaining.

blocks.label: HashMap Internal Node Structure (Simplified from JDK Source)
lines: // Simplified representation of HashMap's internal Node (Java 8+)
static class Node<K, V> implements Map.Entry<K, V> {
final int    hash;   // cached hash of the key
final K      key;    // the key — may be null (stored at index 0)
V            value;  // the value — may be null
Node<K,V>    next;   // next node in the same bucket chain
// When chain length > TREEIFY_THRESHOLD (8) AND table.length >= 64:
// Node<K,V> is promoted to TreeNode<K,V> — a Red-Black Tree node
static final class TreeNode<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap.Entry<K, V> {
transient Node<K,V>[] table;     // the bucket array (length always power of two)
transient int         size;       // total number of key-value entries
int                   threshold;  // size at which rehash occurs (capacity × loadFactor)
static final int DEFAULT_INITIAL_CAPACITY = 16;   // must be power of two
static final int TREEIFY_THRESHOLD        = 8;    // chain → tree
static final int UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD      = 6;    // tree → chain
static final int MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY     = 64;   // table must be this big to treeify

blocks.text: Why power-of-two capacity? HashMap always keeps its bucket array length as a power of two (16, 32, 64, …). This allows the bucket index to be computed with an ultra-fast bitwise AND — index = hash & (capacity - 1) — instead of the slower modulo operation (%) used by Hashtable. The hash spreading step (h ^ (h >>> 16)) compensates for the fact that low-bit patterns in power-of-two tables can cause clustering with poor hashCode() implementations.
HashMap sits cleanly within the modern Java Collections Framework hierarchy, extending AbstractMap and implementing the Map interface — with no legacy baggage unlike Hashtable.

sections.title: Load Factor and Rehashing in HashMap

blocks.text: Two concepts directly govern HashMap's performance characteristics: load factor and rehashing. Getting these right — especially for known-size use cases — can dramatically reduce memory allocations and GC pressure in production applications.

items.text: — A float between 0.0 and 1.0 that determines the fill-ratio at which the bucket array is resized. Default is 0.75f. Formula: threshold = capacity × loadFactor. With defaults: threshold = 16 × 0.75 = 12. The 13th insertion triggers rehashing.

— When size exceeds threshold, HashMap creates a new bucket array exactly 2× the current capacity (e.g., 16 → 32 → 64 → …) — always a power of two. Every existing entry is re-inserted into the new array using the new index calculation. Rehashing is O(n). Unlike Hashtable, HashMap rehashing is single-threaded (no lock) and the new capacity formula is simply oldCapacity << 1.
— Table stays sparse → very few collisions → fast lookups. Trade-off: higher memory usage and more frequent rehashing. Use when access speed is critical and memory is plentiful.
— Table stays dense → memory-efficient. Trade-off: more collisions → longer chains → slower lookups. Treeification kicks in for the worst buckets, but overall throughput still degrades.

— If the final map size is known, construct with: new HashMap<>(expectedSize / 0.75 + 1). This sets the initial capacity high enough that no rehashing occurs, avoiding the O(n) resize cost entirely. Example: for 100 entries → new HashMap<>(135).

sections.title: HashMap vs Hashtable vs LinkedHashMap vs TreeMap

blocks.text: Choosing the right Map implementation is one of the most impactful design decisions in Java. Here is a complete comparison to help you choose correctly every time.

rows: Array of Node chains + Red-Black Trees (Java 8+)

blocks.text: Decision Guide: Default to HashMap for all single-threaded Map needs. Choose LinkedHashMap when iteration order matters (e.g., building an LRU cache). Choose TreeMap when keys need to be sorted or you need range operations like subMap(), headMap(), or tailMap(). For multi-threaded scenarios, use ConcurrentHashMap (unordered) or ConcurrentSkipListMap (sorted). Avoid Hashtable in all new code.

sections.title: Null Key and Null Value Handling in HashMap

blocks.text: One of HashMap's most distinctive features is its deliberate support for null keys and null values. Understanding exactly how this works — and where it can cause subtle bugs — is important for every Java developer.

blocks.text: The null ambiguity trap: get(key) returns null when (a) the key is absent, or (b) the key is present but mapped to a null value. These two cases are indistinguishable from the return value alone. Always use containsKey() when you need to tell them apart, or prefer getOrDefault() to guarantee a non-null fallback for missing keys.

HashMap supports multiple iteration styles. Always prefer entrySet() or forEach — they are both more efficient and more readable than keySet()-based iteration (which requires a get() lookup for each key).

blocks.text: HashMap is fully generic and works with any object as key or value. When using a custom class as a key, you must correctly override both hashCode() and equals(). Failing to do so is one of the most common — and hardest-to-debug — bugs in Java Map usage.

blocks.text: Following these practices ensures that your HashMap usage is correct, performant, and maintainable — whether in single-threaded utilities or complex enterprise applications.

items.text: — Always declare variables as Map<K,V> rather than HashMap<K,V>. This decouples your code from the implementation and allows swapping to LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, or ConcurrentHashMap with a single line change: Map<String, Integer> scores = new HashMap<>();

— If the approximate number of entries is known, use: new HashMap<>(expectedSize / 0.75 + 1). This prevents rehashing entirely, saving O(n) resize operations and reducing GC pressure. For 1000 expected entries: new HashMap<>(1335).

items.strong: ✅ 3. Always Override hashCode() and equals() for Custom Keys
items.text: — Both methods must be consistent: if a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode(). Using IDE-generated or Objects.hash() implementations is recommended. Never use mutable fields in hashCode() computation for keys — changing a key's state after insertion makes it unretrievable.

items.strong: ✅ 4. Use getOrDefault() Instead of get() + null Check
items.text: — Prefer map.getOrDefault(key, defaultValue) over if (map.get(key) != null). The former is cleaner and handles the null-value ambiguity case correctly. For maps that may hold null values, use containsKey() to check existence.

— Instead of checking containsKey() then calling put(), use computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()). It is atomic enough for single-threaded code and expresses intent more clearly. Example: map.computeIfAbsent("group", k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(item);

— Never iterate with keySet() and call get() for each key — that's two lookups per entry. Use entrySet() or forEach(BiConsumer) which provides direct access to both key and value in a single traversal.

items.strong: ❌ 7. Do Not Use HashMap in Multi-Threaded Code Without Synchronization
items.text: — HashMap is not thread-safe. Concurrent modifications can cause infinite loops during rehash, data loss, or ConcurrentModificationException. Use ConcurrentHashMap for shared state between threads — never Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>()) which suffers the same coarse-locking problem as Hashtable.

items.strong: ❌ 8. Do Not Use Mutable Objects as HashMap Keys
items.text: — If a key object's fields change after insertion, its hashCode() changes, placing it in a different bucket. The original entry becomes permanently unreachable (memory leak). Always use immutable objects — String, Integer, enums, or custom immutable classes — as HashMap keys.

HashMap is the workhorse of Java's Collections Framework — flexible, fast, and feature-rich. But like every data structure, it has specific trade-offs you must understand to use it correctly.

pros.title: O(1) Average-Case Performance
pros.text: get() and put() both run in O(1) average time due to direct bucket-index computation. In the rare worst case (all keys collide into one bucket), performance degrades to O(n) for a plain linked-list chain — but Java 8's treeification caps this at O(log n) for large collision chains.

pros.title: Null Key and Null Value Support
pros.text: Unlike Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap, HashMap accepts one null key and any number of null values. This flexibility is valuable when null is a meaningful sentinel in your data model — e.g., representing 'not yet assigned' or 'config not set'.

pros.title: Rich Java 8+ API
pros.text: compute(), computeIfAbsent(), computeIfPresent(), merge(), replaceAll(), and forEach() make HashMap a powerful tool for functional-style data transformation without needing to manually iterate and conditionally update entries.

pros.title: Java 8 Treeification
pros.text: The automatic conversion of long collision chains to Red-Black Trees (when chain length > 8 AND table capacity >= 64) protects against hash-flooding attacks and adversarial inputs. Worst-case lookup is O(log n) instead of O(n).

pros.title: No Synchronization Overhead
pros.text: HashMap has zero locking overhead in single-threaded code. Unlike Hashtable — which acquires and releases a monitor lock on every method call — HashMap performs pure computation, making it measurably faster in profiling benchmarks for single-threaded workloads.

pros.title: Memory-Efficient Power-of-Two Resizing
pros.text: The bucket index is computed with bitwise AND (hash & (capacity-1)), which is faster than modulo. The capacity always doubles during resize, minimizing the number of resize events. Hash spreading (XOR with right-shifted bits) compensates for poor hashCode distributions.

cons.title: Not Thread-Safe
cons.text: Concurrent modification by multiple threads without external synchronization can cause data corruption, lost updates, or even infinite loops during rehashing. This is the most critical limitation — never share a HashMap across threads without ConcurrentHashMap or explicit synchronization.

cons.title: No Guaranteed Iteration Order
cons.text: HashMap provides no ordering guarantees. Iteration order appears random, can vary across JVM implementations, and can change after a rehash. If predictable order is needed, LinkedHashMap (insertion order) or TreeMap (sorted order) must be used instead.

cons.title: null Ambiguity on get()
cons.text: get(key) returns null both when the key is absent and when the key maps to a null value. This ambiguity requires extra containsKey() calls to distinguish, adding verbosity and a potential source of bugs for developers who forget this behavior.

cons.title: Rehashing Cost and GC Pressure
cons.text: When the load factor threshold is exceeded, rehashing creates a new backing array 2× the size and re-inserts all entries. For large maps, this is O(n) in both time and memory — the old and new arrays coexist temporarily, doubling memory usage at peak. Pre-sizing eliminates this risk.

cons.title: Broken Keys from Mutable Objects
cons.text: If a key object's state changes after insertion (altering its hashCode()), the entry becomes permanently unreachable — it sits in the wrong bucket, creating a memory leak and a missing entry. Always use immutable key objects (String, Integer, enums, or custom @Immutable classes).

cons.title: hashCode() Quality Dependency
cons.text: HashMap's performance is entirely dependent on the quality of keys' hashCode() implementations. A poor hashCode() that returns the same value for all keys collapses the HashMap into a single linked list (O(n) lookups), negating all benefits. Well-distributed hash codes are essential.

blocks.text: These are the most frequently asked interview questions on Java HashMap in Java developer interviews — from junior to senior level. HashMap internals are among the most tested topics in Java collections interviews.

items.q: Q1. How does HashMap work internally in Java?
items.a: HashMap stores entries in an array of Node buckets. Each bucket is the head of a linked list (or Red-Black Tree in Java 8+). For each put(key, value): (1) If key is null, store at index 0. Otherwise, compute hash = key.hashCode() XOR (hashCode >>> 16) for bit spreading. (2) Compute bucket index = hash & (capacity - 1) using fast bitwise AND. (3) Scan the bucket chain using equals() — update if found, append new Node if not. (4) If chain length > TREEIFY_THRESHOLD (8) and table >= 64, convert to Red-Black Tree. (5) If size > threshold, resize (double capacity).

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between HashMap and Hashtable?
items.a: Key differences: (1) Thread Safety — HashMap is not synchronized; Hashtable is (all methods). (2) Null — HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values; Hashtable allows neither. (3) Performance — HashMap is faster (no lock overhead). (4) Legacy — Hashtable extends Dictionary (Java 1.0 legacy); HashMap extends AbstractMap (Java 1.2, modern). (5) Initial Capacity — HashMap: 16 (power of two), Hashtable: 11 (prime). (6) Iteration — HashMap: fail-fast Iterator; Hashtable: Enumeration + Iterator.

items.q: Q3. What happens when two keys have the same hashCode in HashMap?
items.a: This is a hash collision. Both entries land in the same bucket. HashMap resolves collisions using separate chaining — entries with the same bucket index are stored in a linked list (Node chain). To find or insert an entry, HashMap scans the chain using equals(). In Java 8+, if a chain grows beyond 8 entries and the table capacity is >= 64, the chain is treeified into a Red-Black Tree for O(log n) instead of O(n) worst-case lookup.

items.q: Q4. What is treeification in HashMap? When does it happen?
items.a: Treeification is a Java 8 optimization where a long linked-list chain in a bucket is converted into a Red-Black Tree. It happens when: (1) A single bucket's chain length exceeds TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8 entries AND (2) The total table capacity is >= MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY = 64. If condition (2) is not met, HashMap resizes (doubles capacity) instead of treeifying — hoping that resizing redistributes the colliding keys. The tree is converted back to a linked list (untreeified) when the entry count in a bucket falls below UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 6.

items.q: Q5. Why does HashMap use a power-of-two capacity?
items.a: Power-of-two capacity enables the bucket index to be computed with a single bitwise AND operation: index = hash & (capacity - 1). This is significantly faster than the modulo operation (%) used by Hashtable. Since capacity is always a power of two, (capacity - 1) is a bitmask of all 1s (e.g., 16-1=15=0b1111), making index computation equivalent to taking the lowest log2(capacity) bits of the hash. The hash spreading step (h ^ h>>>16) compensates for any clustering introduced by this truncation.

items.q: Q6. What is the default initial capacity and load factor of HashMap?
items.a: Default initial capacity = 16 (power of two). Default load factor = 0.75. Initial threshold = 16 × 0.75 = 12. Rehashing is triggered when the 13th entry is inserted. During rehash, capacity doubles: 16 → 32 → 64 → … New threshold = new_capacity × loadFactor. Compare to Hashtable: capacity=11 (prime), same load factor 0.75, threshold=8.

items.q: Q7. Can HashMap have duplicate keys?
items.a: No. HashMap does not allow duplicate keys. If you put() with a key that already exists, the old value is overwritten and the old value is returned. The size does not increase. This is consistent with the Map contract: each key maps to exactly one value. To store multiple values per key, use a Map<K, List<V>> or a Guava Multimap.

items.q: Q8. Is HashMap fail-fast? What does that mean?
items.a: Yes. HashMap's iterators (via keySet(), values(), entrySet()) are fail-fast. If the map is structurally modified (any put, remove, or clear that changes the entry count) during iteration — other than through the iterator's own remove() — a ConcurrentModificationException is thrown. This is detected via an internal modCount counter that is incremented on every structural modification and checked at the start of each Iterator.next() call. Fail-fast behavior is a best-effort safeguard for detecting concurrent modification bugs, not a hard guarantee.

items.q: Q9. How does HashMap handle the null key?
items.a: HashMap specifically handles null keys in a dedicated code path. If key == null, the entry is always stored at bucket index 0 — bypassing the hashCode() computation entirely (since null.hashCode() would throw NullPointerException). The null key slot at index 0 behaves like any other bucket: it can hold a linked list/tree of entries (though typically just one, since only one null key is allowed). get(null) similarly bypasses hash computation and looks directly at bucket 0.

items.q: Q10. Why should HashMap keys be immutable?
items.a: HashMap computes and uses a key's hashCode() at insertion time to determine its bucket. If the key object's state changes after insertion (mutable fields affecting hashCode()), the key would hash to a different bucket. When you later try to get() or containsKey() with the same object reference, HashMap computes the new hashCode(), looks in the wrong bucket, finds nothing, and returns null — even though the entry still exists (in the old bucket). This is a silent memory leak and a hard-to-debug bug. The safest keys are immutable: String, Integer, enums, or custom classes with final fields.

blocks.text: Test your understanding of HashMap with these practice questions covering output prediction, design decisions, and internal behavior.

items.a: Output: 2 30. HashMap does not allow duplicate keys. The second put("A", 30) overwrites the first value 10 with 30. The map has only 2 entries ("A" and "B"), so size() returns 2. get("A") returns the latest value 30.
Output: 1 updated. Only one null key is allowed. The second put(null, "updated") overwrites the first value "zero". size() is 1 because there is still only one entry (the null key entry).

items.q: 3. You need to count character frequencies in a String using HashMap. Write the most concise correct approach using Java 8 methods.
items.a: Use merge(): Map<Character, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>(); for (char c : str.toCharArray()) { freq.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum); }  Alternatively: computeIfAbsent is more verbose here. merge() is the most idiomatic approach — it handles both the 'key absent' (insert 1) and 'key present' (add 1 to existing) cases in a single call.

items.q: 4. A HashMap has initialCapacity=16, loadFactor=0.75. After how many put() calls does the first rehash occur? What is the new capacity?
items.a: Threshold = floor(16 × 0.75) = 12. Rehashing is triggered when size exceeds the threshold — i.e., when the 13th distinct entry is inserted. After the 13th put(), size becomes 13 > 12, triggering resize(). New capacity = 16 × 2 = 32 (always doubles, always power of two). New threshold = 32 × 0.75 = 24.

Output: 'color not found' — but this is WRONG / a bug. The key "color" IS in the map — it just maps to null. hm.get("color") returns null because the value is null, not because the key is absent. The correct check is: if (hm.containsKey("color")) { System.out.println("color is set to: " + hm.get("color")); }. This is the classic null-value ambiguity trap in HashMap.

items.q: 6. Two HashMap keys have hashCode() returning the same value but equals() returning false. What happens when both are put into a HashMap?
items.a: Both entries are stored in the same bucket (same hash → same index). In the bucket's linked list (or tree), they appear as separate nodes because equals() returns false for them — the scan finds no match and appends a new Node. Both entries coexist in the map. size() = 2. This is a collision — it does not corrupt data, but it degrades performance if many keys collide this way (long chain → O(n) or O(log n) after treeification).

items.q:
7. Explain why the following code is NOT thread-safe even when using ConcurrentHashMap:
if (!map.containsKey(key)) { map.put(key, value); }
items.a: This is a check-then-act compound operation. Even with ConcurrentHashMap, the containsKey() and put() calls are individually atomic, but the combination is not. Between containsKey() returning false for Thread A and Thread A calling put(), Thread B can also call containsKey() (gets false), then both threads call put() — resulting in a race. The correct atomic alternative is: map.putIfAbsent(key, value), which is a single atomic operation in ConcurrentHashMap.

items.q: 8. A custom class overrides hashCode() to always return 42 for all instances and equals() correctly. What is the performance impact on a HashMap with 1000 such keys?
items.a: All 1000 entries land in the same bucket (all have hash → same index via 42 & (capacity-1)). The bucket becomes a single chain of 1000 nodes. In Java 7, get() degrades to O(n) = O(1000) — scanning the entire chain. In Java 8+, once the chain exceeds 8 entries AND table capacity >= 64, the chain is treeified into a Red-Black Tree, improving get() to O(log n) = O(log 1000) ≈ O(10). However, this is still drastically worse than O(1). A well-distributed hashCode() is essential for HashMap performance.

sections.title: Conclusion — HashMap as the Foundation of Java Data Storage

blocks.text: HashMap is the backbone of key-value storage in Java. From simple configuration maps to complex in-memory caches and data aggregation pipelines, virtually every non-trivial Java application uses HashMap directly or through frameworks built on top of it. Its O(1) average-case performance, rich Java 8+ API, and null-key flexibility make it the default choice for the vast majority of Map use cases.

Understanding its internals — the power-of-two bucket array, hash spreading, separate chaining, treeification, load factor, and rehashing — is not just academic knowledge. It directly informs decisions about pre-sizing, key design (immutability and hashCode quality), and when to reach for LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, or ConcurrentHashMap instead.

rows: ✅ Use HashMap — fastest, most flexible, modern API
✅ Use LinkedHashMap — extends HashMap, adds ordering
Need sorted key order or range queries
✅ Use TreeMap — O(log n) but always sorted
✅ Use ConcurrentHashMap — fine-grained locking, atomic ops
⚠️ Migrate to HashMap or ConcurrentHashMap gradually
❌ Redesign — always use immutable keys in HashMap

items.q: What is HashMap in Java?
items.a: Java HashMap is a hash table-based implementation of the Map interface in the java.util package. It stores key-value pairs and uses a hash function to determine the storage bucket for each key. HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values, is not synchronized (not thread-safe), and does not guarantee any iteration order. It offers O(1) average-case performance for get() and put() operations. Introduced in Java 1.2 as part of the Collections Framework, it is the most widely used Map implementation in Java.

items.q: What is the difference between HashMap and Hashtable in Java?
items.a: Key differences: (1) Thread Safety — HashMap is not synchronized; Hashtable is synchronized (all methods). (2) Null Handling — HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values; Hashtable allows neither. (3) Performance — HashMap is faster in single-threaded code due to zero synchronization overhead. (4) Legacy — Hashtable is a legacy class from Java 1.0 extending Dictionary; HashMap was added in Java 1.2 extending AbstractMap. (5) Initial Capacity — HashMap defaults to 16 (power of two); Hashtable defaults to 11 (prime). (6) Iteration — HashMap uses fail-fast Iterator; Hashtable supports both Enumeration (legacy) and Iterator.

items.q: How does HashMap handle collisions in Java?
items.a: HashMap handles collisions using separate chaining — each bucket holds a linked list of entries that hash to the same bucket index. In Java 8+, when a single bucket's chain grows beyond 8 entries (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD) and the total table capacity is at least 64, the linked list is converted into a balanced Red-Black Tree, improving worst-case lookup from O(n) to O(log n). When entries are removed and the tree shrinks below 6 nodes (UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD), it converts back to a linked list.

items.q: Can HashMap have null keys or null values?
items.a: Yes. HashMap allows exactly one null key and any number of null values. The null key is always stored in bucket 0 (index 0), bypassing the normal hash computation since null has no hashCode(). Null values are stored normally. This is in contrast to Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap, both of which throw NullPointerException for null keys or null values.

items.q: What is the default capacity and load factor of HashMap?
items.a: HashMap's default initial capacity is 16 (a power of two) and the default load factor is 0.75. The initial threshold is 16 × 0.75 = 12, meaning rehashing is triggered when the 13th entry is inserted. During rehashing, the bucket array doubles in size (e.g., 16 → 32 → 64 → ...), always remaining a power of two. This power-of-two sizing enables fast bitwise AND bucket-index computation instead of the slower modulo operation used by Hashtable.

quickFacts.dd: Yes — exactly one null key allowed
